utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Krajisnik, not to your surprise, but I'll remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony. And, Mr. Krajisnik, I did understand that you had an opportunity to watch the DVD, at least the video, and that it would cause you to make some additional comment or to add to answers you've given before. Mr. Stewart, I may take it that this is the right moment to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, please tell us what we should know about it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I got this DVD. In addition to this interview, there's another interview there as well, and I actually wrote down where the beginning is and where the end is and where the interruption is in this interview. Actually, this interview consists of two different parts. I can tell you exactly what it is. The beginning is at 37 minutes, 50 seconds, and the end, 54.09 -- oh, sorry, sorry. 5 minutes, 46 seconds. And 8 minutes, 23 seconds, that's the end. The interruption is 7 minutes, 21 seconds, and I know exactly where it is. It's where the second part of the more extensive interview starts. It can be seen easily. I viewed it last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask the parties, is there more on the DVD than there is in evidence? If so, parties should consider whether ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, the disk is -- contains one video clip, but it's a compilation of a number of different interviews, as we understand it. So it's one video file, as we understand it, but it does contain a number of different interviews.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course what I'd like to know is whether there's anything on it that is not evidence. If everything is in evidence, then it seems that the relevant point is whether there is a cut somewhere in the middle which could -- might explain what Mr. Krajisnik says: I said more but that's not recorded, it's not broadcasted, at least it's not on this video. Another matter is whether portions of what now seems to be a compilation of -- of interview or interviews, whether portions are not in evidence and whether the parties would consider it of such relevance that they would like to introduce that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the answer is I can't remember. It's simply that this was played an awfully long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can't remember, although P70.A.1, which, on the list of exhibits, is described as the transcript of P70 is a very short item, which suggests that there is a lot of stuff that hasn't been put in evidence. But the Prosecution probably know better than us, Your Honour, because it was their disk in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It may have been our disk in the first place, but I'm not sure what is on this particular disk. However --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The parties are invited to look into the questions that I just raised and to consider that if there is anything on this disk that is not evidence - there is a fair chance there isn't - whether both the fact that there is an interruption somewhere and that it resumes somewhere else, whether that fact and the remainder which is not in evidence should be brought to the attention of the Chamber. Please consider it. And Mr. Stewart is -- if, on this specific point, you would now -- you would have to consult with Mr. Krajisnik. I expect that a favourable decision would be given if you would apply for it. At this moment you first have to look at it and then we'll further see what decisions are to be taken or what further evidence we'll see and hear. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We can probably get Mr. Sladojevic to look at it straight away, Your Honour, if it is possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- I just need it handed back, Your Honour. Mr. Krajisnik has got it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the last copy -- it's the one and only copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I thought we needed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you allow me, I can help you, Mr. President. I viewed this, and we can resolve the problem very expeditiously.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We've got it on the hard drive, Your Honour, it seems, so we're all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Mr. Krajisnik, I invited the parties to look at it. If they say it is of no importance whatsoever and if you would say: I would like to put an additional question to myself, that is to ask about that portion of the video, then we'll hear from that. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I want to ask you whether you know of anything of a number of matters said to have involved Crisis Staffs. Do you, yourself, know anything about a Crisis Staff decision to cut off the water supply in the summer of 1992 to the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of any such decision by the Crisis Staff, or others, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you know anything of any Crisis Staff in Bosnia and Herzegovina evacuating the entire Serbian population in order to prepare for an armed attack?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everything I heard here before this Court are things that I never knew about, the evacuation of the population that the Crisis Staff participated in. And I do not recall a single case that I heard of later, that the Crisis Staff did something like that. If there is a document of this nature, I would be happy to comment on it. But I really do not remember any such decision or any such case.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you, during 19 --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excluding Pale, though, I've already said that, lest there be any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: During 1992 - and I'm asking you about what you knew during that year - did you have any knowledge of any Crisis Staff establishing any detention centre?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all documents show that we didn't know and that I didn't know, except for what was going on around Sarajevo and except for the decisions that we passed in terms of having prisons established as state institutions. As for camps, I found that quite foreign; I mean these prisons outside the law that are referred to here. I'm talking about the period up to August, when the government report came in and when an initiative was taken to have them disbanded. Until then, I knew nothing of it, and there are even MUP reports that they didn't know about it. But I don't want you to think that it goes for the whole year.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: During 1992, did you have any knowledge of Crisis Staffs anywhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Serb Crisis Staffs, ordering the arrest of groups of people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know of any such thing, but I know that the Crisis Staffs were the local authority, that they existed in municipalities. That they did this, that I did not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Sladojevic suggests that in the last answer, which it shows on the transcript, the reference "there are even MUP reports," Mr. Sladojevic suggests that that -- that might have been more specifically qualified by Mr. Krajisnik, the reference to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, where you said "and there are even MUP reports that they didn't know about it," it's suggested that you said something more. Could you tell us what, in addition to what I just read, you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In mid-August -- or was it in July? The MUP set up some commissions, and they went to tour the camps. They received reports, and once these reports came in, it became obvious that the MUP had not known about these camps earlier on. We discussed it then, and it was after that that the camps were disbanded. My point was that up until then, even the MUP did not know anything about this, which can be seen from the documents about the camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, did you during 1992 have any knowledge of Crisis Staffs authorising transfer of prisoners in and out of detention centres?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Detention centres and what was the other word? I didn't understand it. No, I knew that there were commissions for the exchange of prisoners. As for the role of Crisis Staffs, I didn't know about that. I didn't know that they had anything to do with the prisoners. As far as I can remember, the commissions were in different corps. Every corps had its own commission for the exchange of prisoners, and then there was this central commission. At that time I didn't know of it, but later on I heard about that, that is to say that I found out later in connection with the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, did you in 1991 or 1992 have any personal knowledge of Crisis Staffs ordering non-Serbs to be removed from municipal positions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know about that. When I'm talking about Crisis Staffs, I'm saying that I did not know about that, and it would be very important to look at a period or, rather, the period up until August and the period after August, if we are talking about 1992. But as for all of 1992, well, first and foremost, they did not exist later. But I was not aware of their activities of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps you would explain to the Trial Chamber -- you've a couple of times today given answers which indicate a change in your knowledge around August 1992 of a number of matters. Could you perhaps make it clear to the Trial Chamber what change there was in August 1992, in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you so much for this question. All the time, up until the end of July or the beginning of August, the government tried to obtain information as to what was going on on the ground in order to have information. Rumours were coming in, and in respect of that, they formed three commissions; one for Herzegovina, as far as I know; one for Krajina; one for Semberija. And some time in the month of August, they got these reports. The reports were not exactly terrible, but certain irregularities were established. There was a debate in the government and in the Presidency in connection with these reports. I attended as a guest, and a resolute order was issued then to have all the irregularities redressed to see who the culprits are and to have appropriate measures taken. That can be seen from all the records. I think this was the 6th of August, or something like that, but until then the Presidency did not know about this, but I in particular did not have any knowledge of any such thing. I would like to remind you that on the 10th of August, the Assembly was held in Banja Luka and an MP put a question concerning prisoners. It was not on the agenda then, so it would be very important for me to clarify why this was not put on the agenda then, because this was actually held against the president of the Assembly then. Later on prisons were disbanded and better conditions were created when better-quality information was obtained. That is why I am saying that it is important to distinguish between these different periods of time. What I possibly did know had to do with the area around Sarajevo, but as for these problematic prisons that were before this court, Sratke [phoen], whatever, I didn't know anything about this. Kula is the only legal prison that I knew of, that I thought this was something normal. I did not think that there was anything irregular going on there, and after all, this was not within the scope of my authority, but it was the government and the appropriate ministries that were supposed to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, were you aware in 1991 or 1992 of Crisis Staffs ordering the removal of non-Serbs from private employment positions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, although there were very few private companies, but I didn't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like you to have, please, an exhibit which is P529, binder 5, tab 221. Now, this is a report on the work of the Municipal Assembly and War Presidency from Bosanska Krupa covering a period, it says, of the 1st of January, 1992, to 20th of April, 1993, and dated April 1993. First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, did you at any time in 1991, first of all, ever visit Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not visit Bosanska Krupa. As a matter of fact, I never visited Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that answered my next question. Mr. Krajisnik, it's a relatively long report, but one thing it does record, and that's on -- you needn't worry too much, Mr. Krajisnik, about the specific passages unless I ask you to. But on the English, at page 4 at the end of the long first paragraph, first full paragraph, it says: "The Crisis Staff of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa began its work at the beginning of January 1992 as the situation was becoming increasingly complex." It's a fairly simple sentence, Mr. Krajisnik, so don't worry too much about finding the text. Were you aware in January 1992 that a Crisis Staff had been established in Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. I was supposed to go to Bosanska Krupa. I was invited to the opening of a church, but Mrs. Plavsic went. And I know that I did not hear of information of this kind from her either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you, between - let's try and be specific - between January 1992 and the beginning of the war, hear anything about what was happening in Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of two cases that occurred in that area. I don't know when this was. One was the arrest of Milan Martic in Otoka. I think that the municipality is Bosanska Krupa. And the other case was an excessive incident, namely that the monument to Branko Copic, the bust of Branko Copic, was ruined and there was this small conflict between the Serbs and Muslims in Bosanska Krupa. I knew that indirectly, if I can put it that way. And perhaps it was even a telephone conversation that I had with someone, but now I probably cannot remember. This was a political problem that was supposed to be resolved between the Serb and the Muslim side, and the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina took part in solving this problem as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, there's a paragraph, Mr. Krajisnik, that begins -- it's on page 5 of the English. It begins: "The War Presidency made an assessment of the situation..." Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll start reading it, Mr. Krajisnik, and we'll see it. It's on page 4, it's the top paragraph on page 4. Do you see: "The War Presidency made an assessment of the situation..."?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "The War Presidency made an assessment of the situation," and the time period being talked about here, apparently from the document, is certainly at the earliest April of 1992, "and took the only feasible and appropriate decision at the time regarding the Muslim population that remained in enclaves in the Serbian territory on the right bank of the Una. First came the decision on the surrender of arms in all Muslim areas in order to free some of the units of the Serbian Territorial Defence which were maintaining a blockade of Muslim villages. This decision was very poorly implemented. No agreement was reached in the Ostruznica and Badic area. The weak response or total disregard of Muslims to the call for surrender of arms and Alija's threat that Krupa must become green, whatever the cost, forced the War Presidency of the Serbian municipality to offer Muslims two options. They could organise themselves and, with our guarantees and full protection, move out to the destination of their transfer, or this would be done by military means. All Muslim villages in the central regions accepted the temporary transfer, provided they could take along all their movable property." Mr. Krajisnik, first of all, there's a reference to -- there to Alija's threat that Krupa must become green, whatever the cost, and we know by now "what must become green" means, "green" for Muslim. First of all, do you know or did you know in 1992 anything at all about a threat by Mr. Izetbegovic - we take it it's him - that Krupa must become green?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that he made such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you aware in 1992 of any similar types of threat or statement by Mr. Izetbegovic in relation to any municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1990 there was an immoderate remark by Mr. Izetbegovic about that area; but in 1991 I don't recall him making any statements about this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The immoderate remark in 1990, first of all, in what circumstances was it made? Was it a -- on a media or was it in a meeting or where?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At an election rally in Velika Kladusa, which was held before the elections, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic said that the Muslims would defend Bosnia with weapons. He noted this in his memoirs, in his book. This was immoderate because 1990 was the beginning; the situation was bad. The reason it was immoderate was that this area was raw. It was a highly sensitive area, because in World War II there had been a terrible conflict there and genocide had been perpetrated against the Serbs. I learned what the reference to the dead meant later on. Mr. Vjestica gave an interview to the Office of the Prosecutor in which he explained that before World War II the proportion of Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's okay. I'll ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that I was to say everything I knew; that's why I was explaining this. He said that the ratio of Serbs to Muslims was 75 per cent Muslims, 25 per cent Serbs, whereas now it was the other way around. And he also explained what is stated here because he was asked this by the Prosecution. He said that he had two school friends who were Muslims who came to see him and asked him for his assistance in moving out of the area. That's what I knew about all this. At the time I knew only what he said at the Assembly on the 12th of May, and I cannot explain how I understood his speech. And it corresponds to what he said to the Office of the Prosecutor. He is a robust man, he's rather radical, but he's also a very warm and gentle person; however, his speeches were quite belligerent. I'm referring to Miroslav Vjestica, the deputy from Krupa. The Office of the Prosecutor gave this interview to my Defence and my Defence showed it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Krajisnik, just moving on to the point here that's in the text. It refers to the Muslims in Bosanska Krupa having been given the two options to organise themselves and move out or it would be done by military means. First of all, were you aware of any such option being given to Muslims in Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992 were you aware of any such option or a similar option being given by Serbs to Muslims in any other municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, on the 12th of May, I heard from Mr. Vjestica at the Assembly that all the Muslims had left their areas. And I even understood that they were "assisted" to leave and that their departure was not completely voluntary. Later on he explained it differently, but I did not hear anything similar from anybody else. I only heard about it at the Assembly, and I can explain my understanding of it at the time. I'm referring to the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I inquire why assisted -- perhaps I missed something -- why "assisted" appears in inverted commas at line 18 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's because the translator said that that is what Mr. Krajisnik said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I just want to be clear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik said assisted between -- at least that's how it was translated, and that's what I heard in English and that is what --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, that answers my question. I just noticed and wanted to be clear. Just an inquiry, Your Honour, to be dealt with. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- Mr. Krajisnik, the -- you said that their departure was not completely voluntary. What -- what did you understand as -- as being -- well, if you like, the -- what it was that made their departure not completely voluntary?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that area, as I understood him to say, the Serbs all went to Serb territory and the Muslims all went to their own territory. And nobody did this because they wanted to. Mr. Abdic said, and it's in one of his newspaper interviews, that everyone should return to his own home because this was artificial. That's why I said "assisted." It wasn't because people really wanted that, but he was not successful because they realised it wasn't realistic at that point in time. But everybody was talking about everybody returning to their own homes, and that's what the meeting between Mr. Abdic, Mr. Vjestica, and the others was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you -- no. Just leaving Bosanska Krupa as a specific municipality for the moment. In 1992, did you know anything about any Crisis Staff establishing anything going under the label of a travel agency or an exchange agency which had anything to do with the movements of Muslims out of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one point in time - and this was in the second half of 1992 - I learned that there was an agency, either in Banja Luka or in Bijeljina. This was not an agency run by the Crisis Staff; it was a privately owned agency. After the decision or announcement, and as I mentioned it was the International Red Cross who also said that, people could leave certain areas where there was a threat. There were many complaints about the work of that agency, and I think that later on it was closed down because people were working in their own personal interest. And I think that the deputies objected to this at a session of the Assembly, but this happened later, perhaps in the second half of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I ask one additional question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, when you said they were "assisted," what do you mean by that? Do I have to understand that to be that the Serbs were more or less pressured to go to the Serb area and, if need be, for that purpose, leave the places where they had lived until that moment and, similarly, the Muslims? Or -- how do I have to understand the assistance? Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, the transcript says: Do I have to understand that to be that the Serbs were more or less pressured to go to the Serb area and not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And similarly the Muslims. I was talking about all inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] His Honour is a clever man and he had put a very good question. Because there was reciprocity. Your Honour, I understand all these questions. You see, when Mr. Vjestica was explaining things, he was introducing a little bit his radical views and his boasting. He said that he had been asked by his neighbours to go over, but he was trying to make himself sound important. He had helped them, in his view. But I didn't think that this was voluntary. People were not just fleeing the war, but the Serbs "helped them." They didn't really help them, but people wouldn't have left if there hadn't been a war and if they hadn't been afraid. That's how I understood it and that's why I said "assisted." Your Honour was right, but I was speaking about Mr. Vjestica when I said this and what my impression was of his statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To say it in simple words: They had no other choice than to leave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. You see, it was actually established later that they asked to leave. To what extent this was voluntary and to what extent there was objective fear, that's another question. But nobody would have left the area had there not been a war and were they not afraid. Whether they were intentionally intimidated, that's a different matter, but those who "assisted," these people in leaving were not sad because these people were leaving. So the impression one gets is that this was not all proper. One cannot amnesty it; that's why there was a meeting with Mr. Abdic about all this. They were discussing what to do with the Serbs and what to do with the Muslims. So that -- I tried to explain what my impression of all this was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Your Honour, there's something on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, was your -- when you were hearing about these matters from Mr. Vjestica, was it your understanding that Serbs in his municipality had been behaving in some way improperly towards Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. I knew every deputy as well as I know myself, and when one of them spoke, I knew whether he was bragging or telling the truth. And I knew that what Mr. Vjestica was saying had to be taken with a big pinch of salt. That was my impression. But if he hadn't explained it as he had to the Prosecution, it would have appeared as if he had expelled the Muslims. But he wasn't speaking the whole truth. He didn't say that he had this meeting with Abdic. When we establish the complete picture, as we are now able to do, we can see that there were individual incidents of expulsion, but it wasn't really expulsion. And I understood that -- well, there was a wartime atmosphere, and he was boasting. And not everyone took what he said to be a fact, because a huge number of Serbs was there on the other side, so this problem was simply cancelled out. We didn't know what to do with the Serbs from the Cazin area. But now the whole truth has come to light. All the pieces of the jig-saw puzzle have come together, but this is only 12 years later. My impression at the time was that he wasn't telling the full truth and that he was simply bragging a little bit, boasting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you had made whatever adjustment you would make for the sort of person Mr. Vjestica was and whether he was likely to be bragging and so on, were you then left with any understanding that Serbs in his municipality had been behaving in some way improperly towards Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it that way. That wasn't my understanding, because the way he presented it was the Serbs have come here, the Muslims have gone there. These people can't go back there, and those people can't come back here. And this was a vocabulary appropriate to war. He did not say: We expelled all the Muslims and the Serbs have remained where they were. He was speaking about a situation that existed at the time. The river Una is a border, we are happy that way, there are no Serbs over there, there are no Muslims over here, and that's a good thing. That's what was in his mind. I would have to have a discussion with him now and ask him what he meant at the time, but that would take us away from our main topic. I knew there was a meeting with Mr. Abdic and him, but we simply did not interfere in these local affairs. We discussed this at the Assembly session because we didn't believe it was just one-sided, that it was just the Serbs who had expelled someone. Far fewer Muslims went over than the number of Serbs who were expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm -- I'd like to ask you a couple of questions to get some, if you like, clear guidelines here. You have mentioned, I think already in your evidence, there is a situation, isn't there, where because there's a war on and because people are afraid, they may have left where they lived with nobody telling them to but the circumstances leading them, through fear, to go somewhere else. You -- you understand, and if I've understood well your previous evidence, you say that that did happen in Bosnia in 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am talking about the Krupa area where Mr. Abdic had a meeting with both sides. It was established that the Serbs had fled from one area and the Muslims had fled from another area. They wanted to return everybody to their own homes. But they said there's a war on now, so it's not realistic to do it at present. They all committed themselves to do this once the war was over. And at the local level they even discussed an exchange of the civilian population. We didn't know that at the time. They said: Let all our people go, we will let all your people go, and that way people will be safe. This is in the minutes of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina when Mr. Sefer Halilovic informed them of this. The aim was to save people because everybody wanted to go to the other side, or to their own side. I mean "their own" under quotation marks. That side where they were in the majority. I think it was on the 20th of June that this session of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina was held where this was discussed. Afterwards there was no more discussion of it. There's -- the same thing is mentioned in Halilovic's book, but it's also in the minutes of the Presidency meeting of Bosnia and Herzegovina. So there are descriptions as to how these events took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, was it your view in mid-1992 that for, let us say, a Muslim to be forced at gunpoint to leave where he or she lived and go to another municipality, forced by a Serb, was wrong, unlawful, not acceptable?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The best way for me to explain it is if I tell you what I know. In my view, every Serb was happy if he could leave a Muslim area and cross over to Serb territory. Because I had this impression, I also understood that the Muslims would be happy if they went over to Muslim territory. I didn't know what the Muslims wanted, but I did know what the Serbs wanted. Many Serbs went into Serb Sarajevo. The number of inhabitants there tripled. People were terrified. They were fleeing the war. Whether anybody "assisted" them, that's a different issue, but it was their desire - I'm speaking about the Serbs now - to reach the free territory where they would be in the majority and, therefore, I assume there would be a similar sentiment on the other side. Nobody wanted to remain a minority and wonder whether some criminal gang was going to come along and kill them. That's why I thought the Muslims wanted this, because I knew what was happening among the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it's you answering the questions and I'm always subject to the guidance of the Trial Chamber. I -- if I may, I'd slightly encourage you not to keep putting words in inverted commas in your answers, which I suggest is not helping to make things clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if Mr. Krajisnik thinks that this clarifies the language that he uses, he's free to do so, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honour's hands. I only had in mind that the last time he -- or one of the times he did it, it gave rise to a question from Your Honour to try to clarify it. And now he's used it again. It really immediately provokes a need for a question to clarify. That's all I had in mind, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I had in mind that Mr. Krajisnik, when he earlier explained what he meant while expressing himself in this way, that we should understand - but please correct me when I'm wrong, Mr. Krajisnik - that we should now understand it in a similar way as you explained it before. No. No correction, so therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional question. Mr. Krajisnik, one thing that strikes me is that you are consistently making a comparison to say: Well, it was not one-sided. I take it that for the Muslims it was the same for the Serbs. Nevertheless, when you talked about what you discussed at the Assembly session and when you said you didn't believe that it was one-sided, you said that it was just the Serbs who had expelled someone. And then you added: "Far fewer Muslims went over than the number of Serbs who were expelled." You're using language there which suggests that Serbs were expelled and that Muslims went over, or did you include in "going over" that they were under a similar pressure as the Serbs, of whom you said they were expelled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was probably speaking fast, so the interpretation was not good enough. Your Honour, I am speaking a session of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina where Mr. Sefer Halilovic provided information to the effect that in the Cazinska Krajina area where Bosanska Krupa is located, on the local level the Serbs and the Muslims were negotiating among themselves about an exchange of the civilian population. And at that session, an exchange of Serbs from Zenica and Banja Luka was mentioned -- I'm adding this now. Mr. Halilovic commented on this. It was then that we spoke about it; afterwards, it never came up again at a Presidency session. The second part of my reply, when I was drawing a parallel, it wasn't a parallel between expulsions of Serbs and Muslims in order to amnesty the Serbian side for expelling the Muslims, if it did that indeed, but I said what my understanding was of the reason why the Muslims were leaving their homes. I said that I had information about why the Serbs were leaving Muslim areas. They were all happy to go to Serb territory, and perhaps there were some "voluntary" departures, and I meant to say that it was under pressure, but even so they were happy to arrive on Serb territory. In Serb Sarajevo, there was so many Serb refugees that the population practically tripled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to stop you because you don't answer my question. My question was not to explain all the circumstances but to explain the language you used, which is that you used the term "expelled" for Serbs and you used the word "went over" for Muslims when you compared the situation of the two. I'm just seeking to understand whether it was your intention to make a distinction to the effect that Serbs who left were expelled and whether Muslims who left went over, which is the Serbs being expelled, there is certain -- there is pressure, there would be force -- well, the proper meaning of the word "expelled," whereas the word "went over" is far more neutral, whether you wanted to make that distinction by using this language, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not what I said, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, then, we'll then check that on the basis of the original -- I'll ask the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just explain what I was trying to say, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but please then concentrate on what I ask you and not the whole of an explanation of the circumstances. I'm asking you about the language you used. And if you say: That's not what I said, please then say what you said and we'll check that then on the original tape. So please focus on the language you used.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I very focussed -- let me just give you one further sentence in clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Serbs who went over to the Serb territory were happy that they had gone over. They did not feel that they had been expelled; they felt happy. That's what I said. And because I had this impression, I thought that the Muslims wanted the same thing; that's the entire philosophy that I was trying to present here, what I've been saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll check the original language you used. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps I can just very briefly say that you -- you know that we have to finish on the Trial Chamber's current directions by the end of tomorrow, don't you? Examination-in-chief --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know what? You know what? Please, let me just tell you something. I am answering the way I can, completely. You asked me what my impression was in terms of how the Muslims left; I don't know how they left. I based my impression on what I saw in the case of the Serbs; that's the whole story. I didn't want to say anything else. I assumed that just the way the Serbs wanted to go over to the other territory, I thought that the Muslims wanted to go to their territory, too. I cannot explain it in any other way. It's easy for me to say I don't know, but I wanted to be of assistance to this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, all I want to say is subject to our duties to the court, the one thing that is quite clear is that Mr. Josse and I are on your side; everybody recognises that. But the -- because we are finishing tomorrow, it just -- Mr. Krajisnik, if you would please, when I ask a question, try to avoid feeling that because of those pressures you've got to include all sorts of other things in order to make sure they're said. I would still, please, invite you, as far as possible, to go with your counsel's questions.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, if you were putting the right questions to me, if you understood the problem, it would be easy for me to answer, but you are asking me to say something -- I mean, if I were to say that the Serbs expelled the Muslims, it wouldn't be right because I don't know about this. So I was just trying to explain what my impression was and I wanted to be of assistance. And I think that's useful. I know exactly what every situation was. There is just this problem of a misunderstanding: You do not understand me. And now whether the interpretation is this way or that way. I am telling you that I am saying the truth, the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to stop you. One of the questions put to you by Mr. Stewart was whether it was your view in mid-1992 that for a Muslim to be forced at gunpoint to leave where he or she lived and go to another municipality, forced by a Serb, whether that was wrong, unlawful, not acceptable. You did just not answer that question. I can imagine that you say: I think it was wrong, but to my knowledge it never happened. Okay, fine, that's two lines, and I think you gave a clear answer to Mr. Stewart. You come with a long story, but you do not answer. You were asked about an opinion, and in that opinion of course there is a suggestion -- your opinion is what you thought at that time. That's even a fact, what was on your mind at that time. To that extent, it's not an opinion, although you formed it as an opinion, perhaps at that time. If you would like to add that it never happened, fine, just add one line but answer the question, please. Mr. Stewart, I gave this as an example; I take it that that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, that's most helpful.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I said 100 times that I don't know anything about this. I mean hypothetically what can I say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But give me concrete questions and I will give concrete answers. I will tell you everything I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Krajisnik, this question, if you say: I never thought about it at that time, so therefore I couldn't tell you what my opinion was because I didn't give it ever any thought and I had no knowledge that it ever happened, that would have been a clear answer to a clear question. So please focus on the questions when answering them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, but I am focussed, Your Honour. Please, I'm answering your question. If I would condemn any person who wanted to expel another person at gunpoint, that is a crime, and I've said that ten times. Who has the right to expel someone at gunpoint?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that answers that question of mine, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'll cut to the chase of exactly where I'm going. At one end of the spectrum there is somebody driving somebody away at gunpoint, which you acknowledge is criminal. It's unacceptable. At the other end of the spectrum is, however unfortunate and tragic it is, the circumstances of war leading people, through fear, to leave, and people can argue about how forced that is, but that's, if you like, at the other end of the spectrum here. My question, then, to you is: Can you give the Trial Chamber some idea of what you in 1992 regarded as acceptable where the line was between what constituted assistance, without inverted commas, if you like, legitimate assistance to people to leave, and where it became something which was not acceptable, that was, in some way, a forced and unlawful way of getting people to leave. Could you -- do you see the question and could you give the Trial Chamber an idea of where you drew that line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you did do that in 1992. Of course I don't know whether it has been --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Even --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but even in your mind there are a lot of matters that I have -- never thought over in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour is absolutely right. If the answer is there was no such line in your head, you had no idea, you can say that, Mr. Krajisnik, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not in 1991, not in 1992, but always. I was always against forcible expulsions of the population. I only thought that someone had the right to -- a voluntary choice to leave if they are in fear and if they want to leave voluntarily. I think they have the right to do that. Everybody was afraid of the war. I gave an example. Quite simply, not at any point in time did I think that anyone had the right to expel someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you give consideration in 1992 to the question whether it was acceptable to -- to interfere or to threaten to interfere with somebody's property rights as a way of encouraging them to leave where they lived?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what the interpretation was like now? I didn't understand any of what you were saying. So if I understand what you're saying that somebody is taking somebody's property away, if somebody is supposed to transfer his property to someone else, well, no, nobody has the right to do that. And Mr. Karadzic said that at the Assembly, too, that if you are doing that kind of thing you will have to annul it, on the 27th of July, that's when he said it. And you have that agreement reached in Pale only in terms of safe-guarding property, but not taking it away. Look at the agreement and you will see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you have knowledge in 1992 of non-Serbs being asked to sign forms anywhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina saying that they were leaving their municipality voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know that, but I heard that on the 27th of July, we were in a hurry to get to the London Conference, that Karadzic heard that from some MP and he objected to that. And that's in the stenographic notes, but I didn't pay any attention to that because I was in a hurry to get to the conference, and I was not aware of any individual cases. Because in Pale, I mean people did that, they were safe-guarding each other's property. You take care of my property, I'll take care of your property. So that was quite a normal thing. We always said that after the war everybody's private property would be returned to whoever it belonged to. Look at the stenographic notes of the 27th of July and you will see it written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you aware in 1992 of Serbs in any municipalities taking steps to ensure that Muslims who left that municipality would never return?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that. I was not aware of these insane ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, were you -- I'm turning to a different topic now. Were you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I just ask you, you have gone through a relatively long list of matters we heard here as evidence and whether Mr. Krajisnik was aware of that. Could I add one item to that list?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in 1992, well, let's say the summer of 1992, and I'll just take one example of which we -- on which we heard evidence, were you ever aware of killings at a larger scale of Muslims not in relation to any combat activity and just, to give you an example, for example, the Koricanske Stijene event where men were taken from buses and a large number of them being directly killed. You certainly remember that evidence, I take it. Did you ever hear about such events --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you aware of this or other similar events that had taken place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as for that incident, I heard of it here. But even if there were a smaller-scale incident, whenever I was present there was an immediate response to check this out, whether it was correct or not. Those were the orders issues and investigations carried out. I know about that. And there -- if there were any indications of crimes having been committed, at any meeting that I attended measures would be taken. I can say now that at every meeting I attended, if something like that was heard measures were taken. As for Koricanske Stijene, I never heard of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, when -- when you were involved in international peace talks and negotiations in May, June, July 1992, were there occasions or even one occasion on which you and your colleagues, Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, offered in the course of those meetings any sort of cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, there was a proposal for a cease-fire that was on the table all the time. The 12th of May, after the 12th of May - I'm talking about Assemblies now - we always asked for that. Not only we, but the international community, too. We always called for a cease-fire in order for the talks to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And in making that offer of a cease-fire in those talks, you and your colleagues were making an offer that you were able to implement, were you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not making these proposals. This was the joint view of our delegation. And practically, as a rule, it was initiated by the international community, and we always accepted that. Except on the 12th of May at the Assembly, I think, where we asked at our own initiative for a cessation of combat activities, for a continuation of negotiations -- well, even if war operations were to continue. However, most of this was mediated by the international community, UNPROFOR, or the European Community. We accepted that, but everything was done through the Main Staff to keep this up, and we always received information. If the Serb side was being accused of something, we would invariably be told that it was the other side that did that, and that that is how the cease-fire was broken. There were these mutual accusations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what was the chain of command by which any cease-fire would be implemented, a cease-fire on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic was commander of the Main Staff, and he did that according to his own line, according to the organisation that was there. He was supposed to receive an order, I don't know how this was, from the Presidency -- or rather, directly from Mr. Karadzic. And that is what was brought to him and what then went down to the lowest level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Krajisnik, there is a -- a intercept of a telephone conversation showing that Mrs. Plavsic made a call -- well, say "made a call," she had a telephone call, we don't know who made it, with Mr. Stanisic on the 14th of May, 1992 in which she ordered him to ensure that the Bosnian Serb forces were to cease fire at 1400 hours sharp, not a minute earlier, not a minute later. Were you aware in 1992, in May, of Mrs. Plavsic giving such orders?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I can explain that telephone conversation because I went through it with Mr. Josse, and in relation to some of the things that were going on at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it probably -- leave on one side any conversations you had with Mr. Josse. If you would, yes, would give the Trial Chamber your explanation and your evidence about what you know about that telephone conversation, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic was in Sarajevo, and she was in contact with UNPROFOR, with Mr. Doyl, and I don't know who else, and they insisted on a cease-fire, and there were mutual accusations bandied about, whether the police from Vrace was firing at the Muslims or were the Muslims firing at the police. You heard a few of these telephone conversations in which the police complained that they were being shelled by the Muslims. Since Mrs. Plavsic had been appointed member of the Presidency, member of the supreme command, on the 12th of May, she knew that. And on the 14th of May, she called the minister of the MUP at Vrace, Mr. Stanisic, and she said to him: I agreed on a cease-fire on our side. I hold you accountable for abiding by this, even if they fire at you, because the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina is going to order their own forces not to fire at you. If they fire at you, let me know and I'm going to inform UNPROFOR. She said to him: I hold you accountable for that, and he was saying that he cannot take the fire any longer because he's under Muslim fire all the time. And she said: Well, even if that is happening, let it be seen but do not respond to fire. She wanted the cease-fire to be established on that day. She went to UNPROFOR later, and UNPROFOR helped her go to Serb territory. At that time, I did not know about this telephone conversation, but I can interpret the conversation that is there and the role of Mrs. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, could you tell me what exhibit number we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can give you the reference, Your Honour. I'm not -- I don't know what exhibit number it is, Your Honour, but it is -- no, Your Honour. I don't know what the exhibit number is, Your Honour. It's the 14th of May, 1992, but we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: During the break, if we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll find it on the 14th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wasn't -- I just didn't want to stop and take time, but we'll try and find it for Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, can we be absolutely clear what your evidence is as to the capacity in which Mrs. Plavsic was purporting to give such an instruction. You said she had been appointed a member of the Presidency, a member of the supreme command; she knew that. Was it in one or both of those capacities or in some other capacity that Mrs. Plavsic was purporting to give that order or instruction to Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic was made in charge of relations with UNPROFOR at one particular meeting. She was in Sarajevo and she was the target of different gangs. She sought UNPROFOR protection and she had contact with them. Then this idea cropped up -- or rather, this task. And she called the MUP at Vrace and the minister answered the phone. She talked to him, first of all as the member of the Presidency who was in charge with relations with UNPROFOR, and she knew that she became a member of the Presidency in Banja Luka, that that is how it became lawful. Now she is trying to make him deal with this seriously, that he should observe this at all costs, but I believe that she did that because she cared first and foremost about the Serb side not being blamed for this and for having the cease-fire observed. Now, what she thought, whether she was doing this as a member of the supreme command, which she was; or as a member of the Presidency, which she was; or as the person in charge of relations with UNPROFOR, which she was. What she had in mind then, I don't know, but on all of these accounts she had the right to order Mr. Stanisic to do that. This is how this conversation took place in order to have the cease-fire observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you know at the time of this telephone conversation or that there was communication on this specific matter between Mrs. Plavsic and Mr. Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember that I was following these matters, and I believed that at that time I did not know anything about this. But I did know that she was in Sarajevo and in a very difficult situation, that in fact she was a prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to hand over to Mr. Josse, so I don't know whether Your Honours would want two minutes of Mr. Josse or would need a break before him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although every minute from Mr. Josse is a pleasure to hear, nevertheless we would first have the break. We will resume at 10 minutes past 4.00. Yes, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, simply this: Could Mr. Krajisnik be handed -- could he be handed the double pension material look at during the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There's no problem with that. And in order to prevent that Mr. Krajisnik has other concerns as well, I can tell him that next Tuesday, between 8.00 and 9.00 to the dentist, has the full support of the Chamber, which would mean for the parties that we would have a start later, and it depends --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- how much Mr. Krajisnik will have to suffer, whether it will be 10.00 or 10.15. Yes, the material may be handed out to Mr. Krajisnik and I think as I said before, there's a favourable inclination of the Chamber to have it discussed with him and of course, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I suspect I'll have to do that at the second break, when he's had a chance to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, approval is given for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at 10 minutes past 4.00

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, it was announced that we would have the pleasure of your examination now. Please proceed -- not to say that it was any less of a pleasure when Mr. Stewart examined the witness, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just -- both parties have ascertained that intercept that was referred to, which as P64A, binder 7, tab 221. That's the one between Mrs. Plavsic and Mico Stanisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, I am going to try and tidy up a few matters that have been left unresolved in the course of questions I have asked you previously. We had got yesterday to the point where Mr. Tieger helpfully made it clear that you hadn't answered a question that I had asked. The question was: Were you aware of the presence of several hundred paramilitaries in Pale in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of any paramilitary formations at Pale at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The last matter in relation to the Muslim population of Pale that I want to ask you about is this: The same witness alleged that he later learnt, after his own departure, that 12 Muslims remained behind in Pale during the war and that they were all killed. From your own knowledge, are you aware of any Muslims who lived in and -- in Pale through the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of one case. We have a statement by a Muslim woman who spent the war at Pale, but I don't know how many of them there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you know her yourself during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I didn't know her. But there is a statement, so I know it's there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any Muslims having been killed in Pale during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any such cases. It was in the purview of the MUP, and whether such things happened, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have redone the documents that were handed out yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: They are on the bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have seen them now without comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We would like numbers attributed to them and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One by one, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps that's a better way of dealing with it because it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, perhaps the registrar could do that whilst I continue the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we could come back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the first document you would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The first document might as well be the one that has the A upon it, which is the one dated the 9th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be D197, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does Your Honour want me to go through them one by one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I take it that you're putting questions about these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then the next one would then be B -- be Crisis Staff document, 11th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be D198, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D198. Then the third one would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is an article from Glas, 17th of April, 1992, the date appears on the text. That would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D199, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next one would be document D, which is a document, an order, from the Pale Crisis Staff. Is that -- it sounds so familiar. It's -- I think it's in evidence already, isn't it, these telephone numbers that were cut off?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The telephone numbers that were cut off is in evidence already, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we don't need D --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I should have spotted that. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then E is a document, the Municipal Assembly of the municipality of Pale, at least the president of it addressing the SDS secretary. That would be -- and that's 12th of June, 1992, would be, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D200, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D200. Next one would be F, which seems to be -- at least that's what your explanation says, the minutes of the Pale Skupstina opstina Pale, that's the Assembly of Pale municipality, 18th of June, 1992, would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D201, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 201. Next one would be G, which is a decision of the Pale Assembly if -- dated the 19th of June, 1992, would be D?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 202, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 202. The next one would be H is a handwritten document described as a request made by ten Muslims sent to the Pale Assembly, Skupstina opstina Pale. And is it correct that it's addressed at Pale SUP, Mr. Josse?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the SUP being the address used here to send something to the Assembly. That would be D?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 203, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 203. And, yes, that was the 22nd of June. Next document --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I notice the next document has an ERN number upon it. I -- I'm afraid I don't know whether it's been exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not on -- let me just see -- yes, because the -- what we find after H, the first page, is a page also handwritten but in apparently a different handwriting. And a stamp on the top of it, Skupstina opstina Pale. It is dated the 22nd of June. Is that part of H, Mr. Josse, or does it belong to I?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Same topic, different document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same -- so we should then make the first one, that is the 22nd of June, 1992, with 12 names on it is D203, perhaps A. And then the next one with a list of 25 names on it, although it seems to other persons are -- oh, no, I see already that's -- yes -- well, next one is, you say, similar document. That would be 203B --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I would say. Next one is I. You say there's an ERN number on it. Do we know whether it's in evidence? Is there any way of searching very quickly?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We've looked and we couldn't find any reference to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You couldn't find it. We'll assign a number to it provisionally. It's a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, no. Could Your Honour give me one moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: P64A, tab 738.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just check whether that's -- whether I have a similar ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There may be another number, Your Honour, P529, Hanson tab 526.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the most important point is, at least, whether it's in evidence, yes or no. 738. Yes. 25th of June, handwritten 0016092. Yes, that's in evidence -- at least perhaps under other numbers as well, but 64A is 738, so it doesn't need a number to be assigned. Then we have J, document J, that should be a letter of the Serbian people from Radovica sent to the Skupstina opstina Pale, also dated the 25th of June, with -- and there I -- Mr. Josse, I see some handwriting on it, but it's cut off at the bottom with a date on it, the 25th of August, 1992. And it's not clear to me whether that's -- has any relevance to the documents. Could you please have a look at that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll check to see if we've got a better copy. That's the best I can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But we provisionally, then, assign the next number. That would be, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D204, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 204. K, document of the 2nd of July, says that it's a decision of the MUP in Pale. Yes, that would be D?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 205, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 205. L is badly legible, but it seems to be an exchange contract Crncalo --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But it's clearly important. I fear it's going to be sent back from the CLSS. Could it be given a number at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, provisionally we'll assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D206, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We've already asked the CLSS to translate as much as they possibly can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if there would be any better copy, of course, that would be preferred. I take it that the next -- the -- is that the back of the document? It seems that it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There's a stamp on it, and it --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: No, Your Honour's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and it's -- it gives same names, at least one of the names -- no, two names on it -- yes, all the names of those who appear on the -- on the front also appear on the back, as far as I can see. Okay. That's -- we take it at this moment that that's the back of the same page?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's what Mr. Sladojevic tells me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then that is part of the document. It doesn't need -- then document M is a list of registered contracts. No date on it, although the entries often are of 1992, at least at the first page. That would be, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D207, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 207. And it seems that the last -- may I just ask you, Mr. Josse, it looks as if it's one page out of a register containing the number 771 up to and including 775. The second page, I take it, is the -- is the right-hand side of that same document. Is that how I should understand it? Yes, it very much seems because we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- columns 1 to 4 on the first page, and 5 to 8 on the second one. And then finally we'd --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'd invite the Court to infer that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then we have, finally, a last page with a stamp on it which seems to be related to that, because it seems to be some stamp of -- at least it comes from Pale. And the date, 22nd of February, 2005, is the date. So we take that to be part of document D207. Then we go to the next one which is N, 6th of July, 1992, decision of the MUP of Pale. Mr. Registrar, that would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D208, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next one, document 6th of July, 1992, report of the Pale MUP regarding the verification of place of residence of Muslim and Croat citizens. Yes, that would be D ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 209, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 209. Next one being document P, 6th of July, 1992, conclusions of the Pale Executive Committee. That would be D ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D210, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, let me just have a look. Yes. Mr. Josse, perhaps with the assistance of Mr. Sladojevic, I see two signatures with what seems to be people with different -- from different organisations, apart from, of course, their names being -- it's described here as conclusions of the Pale Executive Committee. The first seems to say something of the president of this and this and this, and then the second is something like the commander of what seems to be this staff, but not the usual Crisis Staff. Could we just -- could I just check whether the description that is -- these are conclusions of the Pale Executive Committee is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you like Mr. Sladojevic to read the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, to read slowly just the two -- the -- the two lines, two times, in capitals above the names of those two signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "President of the Executive Committee. Commander of the staff of the civilian protection."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then as a matter of fact, on the top of the document it's -- from what I see it just says that it's the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina opstina Pale, without -- no, I see that -- and then there's one line under that which may identify the body from which it -- could Mr. Sladojevic read that as well, which -- just the third line from the top, under opstina Pale it reads --

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Executive Committee."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That has been clarified, so signed by two persons of different bodies, but at the top the Executive Committee. That, Mr. Registrar, would be D ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 211, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 211. Next document would be under Q, date is 7th of July, 1992, described as information of the Pale Executive Committee. Yes, we see that's the same at the top. Sent to the Pale war commission to be handed over to Mrs. Plavsic. That would be D ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, the number I just -- Mr. Registrar just gave for the document which -- we find under P should be 210.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then under Q it would be 211, I take it, Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 211, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 211. And then we go to what we find with an R on it. We leave all the letters on it. They are added by the Defence, otherwise we have to take them out again, but that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right, they're purely there for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So R would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 212, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 212. It's a document of the 10th of July, 1992, described as a conclusion of the Pale Executive Committee. Then under S we find a document, 14th of July, 1992, also from the Pale Executive Committee conclusion would be D ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 213, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 213. Then under T we find a document with the same description but now from the 16th of July, 1992, would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D214, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 214. Then under U we find a document dated the 10th of August, 1992, from the Pale SO, stands for Skupstina opstina, I take it, yes, which is a decision on giving -- of temporary use of free, deserted, and unlawfully occupied houses. That would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D215, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 215. And, finally last one under V is a document dated the 21st of October, 1992. It again is a conclusion originating from the Pale Executive Committee. Please proceed, Mr. Josse --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, I forgot, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be D216, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D216. I take it that translations will be provided as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Prosecution will have an opportunity to object once we have received that. Fortunately here the availability of the witness at a later stage might not be that much of a problem if any further questions would be -- would have to be put to the witness in respect of these documents. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next matter I'd like to clear up, Mr. Krajisnik, is this: Yesterday you mentioned a document or a report prepared by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina which dealt with comparative indicators of population, and that is also on the learned Judges' bench. Could you be given a copy of it, please. If I may briefly explain the position. It's right, isn't it, that this, in fact, is a brochure which you obtained through your own means. It is a brochure that is in both B/C/S and English. We have only copied the English part of it. No doubt you can make available the B/C/S part.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We either do not have it or have insufficient information to identify it. Perhaps we can have an ERN number or some more specific --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It has no ERN number. I've made arrangements for it to be supplied to my learned friends by their office first thing this morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
