utterances.text: That helped, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From a distance, I see that it's the same document as the Judges have.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Krajisnik, it's right that we only have the English here, and I suspect you haven't brought the original with you. There's no reason why you should, because you didn't know I was going to deal with it today. The reason I'm dealing with it today is you mentioned it yesterday. What do you want the Chamber to use it for, please?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I want to draw attention to the fact that this was a brochure issued by the official government of Bosnia-Herzegovina dealing with movements of the population. It can be very useful when drawing conclusions on the part of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could it have a number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D217, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If the Trial Chamber requires, at least for the registry version, the B/C/S part of this brochure, I'll need to ask Mr. Krajisnik to provide it to the Defence team and we will copy it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm also now looking at the Prosecution. We see that we have a cover page which, even in a similar layout, gives the content of it. Does the Prosecution wish this document to -- which is mainly a matter of -- no, not all of it, so some text in it as well. The major part of it are statistics, from what I can see, to receive that in B/C/S as well? Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we can -- I mean, at the moment I can see no reason why we would make that request, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course you'll have an opportunity to further -- it may come as a surprise at this moment, this document. Well, let's say, for whatever reasons, because you think that the English version does not correspond with the original, could we hear from you, well, whether we would say not any later than ten days from now?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can direct the Court's attention to the portion behind the green page, I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have a green page, we do not have a green page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Then apparently we have a B/C/S copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have the B/C/S? Then you have an opportunity to see -- because otherwise it has to be copied again and it saves half a wood, if you would be happy with the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I stand corrected, but my -- the original position is maintained the -- what appeared to be a B/C/S version contained a B/C/S cover page and the rest of the document appears to be essentially the same. So nevertheless -- so one doesn't appear to exist, but as I said before, at the moment I can't see that such a request would be made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any wish should be presented within ten days. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Unless there is something particular, Mr. Krajisnik, you wish to draw to the Trial Chamber's attention about this brochure, I'm going to move on to the Davidovic documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At a certain moment, I take it, Mr. Josse, the Chamber will better understand what it has to do with it because we will not learn by heart all the numbers, and these are statistics which are -- well, not only about what has been the -- one of the subjects of the testimony that is in the composition of the population, but also on a lot of events that happened after the armed conflict, from what I see, such as reconstruction of destroyed houses, et cetera, et cetera. So I don't know exactly what we have to do with that at this moment, but we'll learn that, I take it, at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Unless there's anything you want to add now, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm really sorry I haven't brought the original brochure. You have a copy and I have a copy. It would be quite in order if a copy was given to the OTP and to the Trial Chamber. Yesterday I spoke --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it seems that everyone for the time being accepts that there is a B/C/S original, which we can't read anyhow, so please tell us what you'd like to tell us about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would be easier for me if I had the B/C/S. That's the problem, but very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Krajisnik. I'm sure Mr. Stewart will give me a few minutes tomorrow to return to this document. So put it away. You can bring the original brochure and we'll deal with this tomorrow. Okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it that the untranslated parts that we learn about that as well, so I see the word "sovozverno" [phoen] appearing a lot of times, which I do not know what it is, some of the statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If you bring your -- the original, Mr. Krajisnik, tomorrow, I will ask you some questions about it then. Let's move on then, please, to the documents that have been provided in relation to Mr. Davidovic. Could you be handed a bundle of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, the translations have been done by a member of our team, not Mr. Sladojevic for what it's worth. We accept these translations are not perfect, and if these documents are going to be admitted into evidence, they're going to clearly need to go to the CLSS. Now, Your Honour, we had got to the point in relation to this where there was some discussion between the parties and the Trial Chamber as to what to do with these documents in the light of how the cross-examination of Mr. Davidovic had proceeded. It is the second document in this bundle, which has 2 at the right-hand corner, the B/C/S original which is on the other side of the page, on the back of it, so to speak, that I suspect Mr. Krajisnik particularly wants to comment upon. I would invite him to comment upon it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just first see whether we have the -- we don't have any 2 on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: 2 at the bottom of the page in the English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, on the English. That's authorisation --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- 17th of February, 19 --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- apart from whether there would be any objections at a later stage, Mr. Tieger, you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This document -- I believe this is the document was the subject of at least some discussion between Mr. Josse and myself. Mr. Josse indicated that he -- at that time he wanted to consider the -- one way or another the possible introduction of this document and that -- but we would at that point have -- possibly have further discussion about it. If, indeed, this is the document, I simply -- I'd like to know that. There's no point in having a discussion about it with the witness if the -- if -- and thereafter have a question -- a discussion about its admissibility. So I don't want to put -- I don't think we should put the cart before the horse, if indeed that is the document which has been the subject of our discussion. I believe it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me interrupt. I'm in no doubt that this is the document that Mr. Krajisnik attempted to put to Mr. Davidovic and Ms. Loukas commented on -- the passage in the transcript, Your Honour, alluded to are referred to, in fact, a few days ago. I'm in no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Without giving a final decision on whether the Chamber will admit this document in evidence, yes or no, whether -- without giving any final decision on whether that, for example, would be under the condition that the other witness would have to re-appear, we'll consider that, but we do not stop at this moment, Mr. Josse, in introducing the document with this proviso. Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Before it's given a number, because it may in fact be better to give the documents numbers in chronological order, comment on this document dated the 17th of February, 1994. Why do you say it's significant?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's significant because it's linked to this first document. Mr. Djurkovic was authorised in 1994 to carry out exchanges of the civilian population and prisoners, as far as I can recall. The request for this to be his work obligation is dated 10th of July, 1993. Before that, he could not have engaged in this activity. The authorisation was signed by the government commissioner of Republika Srpska and the state commission for exchanges, people's deputy, Milan Tesic, and it bears the government stamp. It also states that in the heading. The next document from the same time period is signed by the same person and bears the same stamp. So he couldn't have been doing that in 1992, but only after he got this work obligation. I wanted to show all three documents to the witness, but first I wanted him to see this authorisation and to say whether this is, indeed, the relevant document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could those first three documents have numbers then, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be 218, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 218 for the document dated the 10th of July, 1993, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document dated the 17th February, 1994, Your Honours, would be D219.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. And then --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The third one dated 18th November, 1994, would be D220.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: That takes us, Mr. Krajisnik, to the next document in the bundle, which is dated the 4th of July of 1995. What, if anything, is of significance of that? It's the one that's a request for Muslim civilians --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- in the corridor of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers to the commission submitting a request to the corps in Bijeljina, that is to say, to the Army of Republika Srpska, to its commander, Novica Simic, for him to make it possible for them to allow the civilian Muslim population to go from Tuzla to Bijeljina. There is an explanation here and a signature -- or rather, signatures of the members of the commission. So this is, by way of an example, as to how they worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that have a number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be D221, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then we have, in fact, a document going back almost two years in time, the 4th of September, 1993, which is again a transit document signed by Colonel Tomic. What does that show?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that shows that at that time the central commission gave its approval to the regional commission for a convoy to pass through their territory. This does not directly relate to this Djurkovic, although that is what is handwritten. But this is an example as to how this convoy could go through the territory. The commission had probably existed even before Mr. Djurkovic became involved in this work.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that have a number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be D222, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And finally, Mr. Krajisnik, there is a document in fact signed by Mr. Davidovic dated the 30th of June, 1992. Is this a document you want to bring to the Trial Chamber's attention?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our investigators got this document from Bijeljina, I don't know from who, and it gives an answer to a question that was put by the Trial Chamber. It has to do with seized cars and how they were allocated. The signature here is of Mr. Davidovic, that he, as chief of police of the Serb MUP, that's what it says here, Milorad Davidovic, that he allocated this seized car to be used for the needs of the Serb MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is very important. In June 1992, according to all available data, he was not the chief; at least that's what he said. He was not the chief in Bijeljina but he was, as he had put it, the representative of Serbia. But here it says that he is the chief of the police of the Serb MUP, who is giving his approval for this seized car. A scene-of-crime technician had examined it and inspected it and probably thought that it had been stolen or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, where does the document say that it's a seized motor car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it says here: Report of -- a crime technician's report on the examination of a car. It says on the 30th of June, 1992, the chief of police asked for a criminal technical examination of a passenger vehicle and to establish the type, make, the number of chassis and so on. This is to say that if it was being processed in this way that this had to do with a seized car that was of unknown provenance. So all of this had to be established in order to know what this was all about. He carried this out, and he, indeed, established this what that was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether that is true or not is another matter, but at least the document doesn't say so, but it's your interpretation of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's my interpretation, and that is what was stated by those who sent it out to us, but whether that was actually the case can be established by some experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could that have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document dated 30th of June, 1992, Your Honours, would be D223.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I just ask about translations. Presumably the Trial Chamber would like these sent to the CLSS to be officially translated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it is to be preferred that we have an official translation of these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you can put those documents away; I'm going to move to a completely different topic. And this relates to the departure of the Serbs from Sarajevo after Dayton. There was a witness who appeared before this Chamber who alleged that you encouraged Serbs to leave, and this witness suggested you even encouraged them to take their graves and traffic signs with them. What do you say on this topic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be a good thing if we were to place the map of Sarajevo here to show where the lines are. It would be easier for the Trial Chamber to understand. I have the map and I think you have it, too, what Muslim Sarajevo was and what Serb Sarajevo was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think there's one map in evidence giving the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that would be good, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know exactly which number it was, but it was not long ago introduced from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. Perhaps a few days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, it was the map that was used in explaining to us what the roads were between Pale and Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't have an up-to-date Defence exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not the map I had in mind. It's -- Mr. Krajisnik, I think it was Mr. Krajisnik who had drawn these lines which come close to Grbavica and the other road, the road through the woods, which was more southerly. It was marked ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We think it might be D190.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's -- yes, that's the map. Could it be put on the ELMO, and we ignore just for the time being the roads and just look at the confrontation lines that were already on the map. So we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is the central part of Sarajevo. This is the part that was held by the Muslim forces. Around is the periphery that was held by the Serbs. And the outskirts of the central part of Sarajevo, that is what was called Serb Sarajevo. This part, the northern part, is the part where many Serbs from Central Bosnia came to. So out of 50 -- out of a population of 50.000, this population grew to, say, 70.000. Most of the Serbs out of 130, and at the plebiscite there were 180, were in the central part of Sarajevo, here. On the periphery there were less Serbs because these are villages. And when Dayton came -- or rather, when the Dayton Agreement was signed, we possessed the periphery. And the central part was actually under the authority of Muslims. Everybody left Sarajevo, those who were under the Muslim government and those who were under the Serb government. The only thing that we advocated was that the Serbs who were in the Serb part of Sarajevo should stay on because we did not have any contact with the Serbs from the central part of Sarajevo, and we also didn't know how they felt. A referendum was held in these peripheral parts where people wanted to remain under their own government, their local government. And that is why what some witnesses said is not true, that any one of us called for the Serbs to leave. Because this witness, who was a protected one, could have been asked the following question: Well, you were there where 90 per cent of the pre-war Serbs were. Why did those Serbs from your part of Sarajevo leave Sarajevo? You received information today that on the entire territory of Sarajevo there is 10 to 12.000. So we were not in contact with these Serbs and we didn't stop them either. We didn't ask them to stay in Sarajevo, but they left nevertheless. I said why the other ones left. But in the central part there were about 100.000 Serbs there before 1992. They left because they wanted to leave Sarajevo at all costs, not to be under the Muslim authorities, because during the war, as they said, they experienced some terrible things. I said that nowadays -- or rather, precisely today the Serb representatives don't want to attend the Assembly meeting. They want a commission to be activated, to activate a commission on the investigation of what happened to Serbs during the war in this Muslim area. There is a list of 3.000 missing Serbs from Sarajevo. And 10.000 are still being looked for. I have exact information on who was taken away and how. As for this part, Serb Sarajevo, those parts that were supposed to come under the Muslim government, too, you have a video-recording here, too, my press conference and of Admiral Layton Smith. We just asked for an extension of time by six months so that people would feel safe, because everybody actually wanted to stay on, but they asked to have a local government of their own. There is a document. Well, this all went slowly. Why? First those who came from the central part of Bosnia-Herzegovina left, those who came to this Serb part, and they were the first to leave as soon as Dayton was signed. There were columns of people leaving, and we kept asking people to stay on. There was this conference in London that was attended by Mr. Aleksa Buha. There is a document to that effect. He asked them to give us a solution based on what was agreed upon in Dayton, before the final solution, and what had been agreed on, that all of Sarajevo should remain united, that it should be transformed and turned into a district. The Muslim side didn't want to accept that. They wanted their own government to take these parts urgently. Therefore, we did not meet with understanding, so in order not to have someone say that we allowed the Serbs to leave Sarajevo, the city Assembly had a meeting and adopted a document. It is everyone's own free will as to whether they want to stay or whether they want to leave, and the majority left Sarajevo. That is why it is completely incorrect that any one of us instigated the Serbs to leave. Your Honours, it is being bandied about in the public that Momcilo Krajisnik said: When you leave, even take traffic signs with you. That is a pure fabrication. In Hadzici, the president of the municipality, who reached an agreement with Bratunac that the entire municipality would move to Bratunac, said at a big rally: We are going to take even traffic signs. When I was persuading the Serbs to stay on I said: Be patient, stay on, things will get better. This is what this gentleman said, Mr. Ratko Radic. As he said: When you leave you can take traffic signs, I meant it figuratively, but don't leave, stay there. So please, this map is important. That's where all the intelligentsia was, all the intellectuals were. After Belgrade, this was the major Serb intellectual centre, so the Serb National Council was here that was headed by Mr. Mirko Pejanovic. They could have done whatever they wanted to to keep people there, but everybody left except for a few individual cases, a few percentage points, if I can put it that way. They went to this side, this other side, and in Dayton we didn't want to have a divided city; now the city is divided, unjustly, but there is this Serb part, whereas all the rest is the Muslim part. And there aren't any Croats or Serbs there. The city of Sarajevo is monolithic, except for individual cases that they are presenting as show cases now in order to show their multi-ethnicity in this way. So this is an example, the Serbs had a choice: To stay or to leave. They were not expelled by the Muslims, but they had some kind of fear and you could not keep people there even theoretically. I don't think that somebody expelled them from Sarajevo, because it would have been 100 times better for them to stay on in Sarajevo rather than live, as they do nowadays, as refugees, under difficult conditions. So this is the whole truth. All these documents are there, so please have a look at them. You will see what the solution for Sarajevo was in Dayton as well. I want to say for the sake of the truth that our delegation had agreed with Mr. Holbrooke on a solution for Sarajevo, and one night it was changed. And I don't think it would be right for me to talk about that now, why this kind of solution was provided for Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, it was a very long answer. Could I have a few precise questions. You were talking about the plebiscite. What plebiscite held at what time? No further explanation, just when approximately and what was the subject.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the end of 1995, the Serbs from the Serb part of Sarajevo expressed their views as to whether they would stay or whether they would leave -- or actually whether they wanted to have their own government. I don't know what the question was, but at any rate they had a plebiscite. It was a kind of referendum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's one. And second, do I understand that those Serbs who were living in Serb-controlled area were encouraged to stay? I understood that to be irrespective of whether they had lived there all of their lives or whether they were from other origin? And second, Serbs living in Muslim-controlled areas were not encouraged to leave that area. Is that, of course very brief, the bottom line of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had contact with Serbs in the Serb part of Sarajevo, and we besieged them to stay on. We did not have contact with Serbs in the Muslim part of Sarajevo, so we were not saying that they should stay or that they should leave because we did not have any contact with them. I went to different rallies, so I spoke to people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about the suggestion Serbs removed the graves of their dead?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is a big sin in Christianity, to move graves. People were carrying graves. They transferred them to Serb territory. My late wife is still in the same grave that is behind Zabrdje. If I were instigating someone to do that kind of thing, first I would have exhumed my wife. It is still there with a broken tombstone, broken by some irresponsible individuals. But every family -- or not every family, many families exhumed their dead, especially the fighters who got killed, and they transferred them to Serb territory. It's not only my wife, but all the deceased Krajisniks are still there, except for one person.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient moment, Your Honour? I know it's a little early, but it would give the Defence a chance to regroup, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's no problem. We'll adjourn until quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to go and see Mr. Krajisnik about the double pensions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is approved.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd now like to -- you've something you'd like to say, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just add one thing in connection with Sarajevo, please, very briefly? Excuse me, but this is a map of Bosnia-Herzegovina. By your leave --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this part here was given to the Serbs by Dayton. This part here to the Croats. After the Dayton Accord, all these people moved, the Croats and Muslims, from here, and the Serbs from here, the Serbs from Sarajevo, although the NATO pact arrived. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This is the map from the brochure, D217, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we recognise that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, I would like to turn to intercepts. Do you still have your bundle of intercepts? And I would like to turn to the intercept that bears the Defence tab number 193. It is P292, KID31469. It's a conversation between you and Mr. Mandic on the 25th of June, 1992. And on the second page in English, towards the top of the page, Mr. Mandic says: "Mr. President." You say: "Yes." He says: "The first part has been mopped up. It was done today." You say: "Did they leave?" He says: "Yes, it's been mopped up." You say: "Huh?" He says: "The first part has been mopped up.". Can you help the Chamber -- two regards, I'm going to ask two questions, if I may, at the same time. First of all, what is he referring to; and secondly, what does he mean when he used the word -- or the expression "mopped up"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is military terminology, meaning that there had been some fighting, and now he thinks that this has been mopped up; in other words, that the opposite sides soldiers are no longer there. This is a little bit mixed up. It's very hard for me to see this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: On the 28th of September of 2004 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, sorry before we go on. I -- just for the record my interpretation of the intercept indicates -- it lists -- it indicates clearly and specifically the word in B/C/S and then the English is "mopped up" or "cleansed" to reflect the possibilities for that translation. And I think the record should reflect it that the intercept bears that translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm afraid I don't have that, and I'm very grateful to my learned friend, and clearly that's very important. Bearing in mind that was the purpose of the question, I'm grateful to him. Could -- I don't know if my learned friend's version is unmarked. If it is, I would ask that it be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm just going to double-check to make sure it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we just also zoom in first on the numbers at the top of the page to see whether they are different? Could I please ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: They are not different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They are the same, but nevertheless there's a different text, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is a different text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we have under the same number different documents, which is not something I'm very pleased with. I would like to check this is material that is already in evidence. Mr. Registrar, could you provide us with P29 -- let me just check what we have here --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I give one other reference whilst that is being done?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because I was going to do this anyway. It was played to this court on the 28th of September, 2004, at page 6228 of the transcript during the course of the evidence of Mr. Kljujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but let's first see what we find in P292. Please continue meanwhile, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, let me go on then, Mr. Krajisnik, because what Mr. Kljujic said about this was -- he used it in some way to support the proposition that you had knowledge that ethnic cleansing was taking place, placing some reliance, as I understand it, on the word that is causing all the difficulty. What do you say about Mr. Kljujic's proposition?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be a good thing to read out the entire intercepted conversation, and I will reply. What the Prosecutor said, this first part, "ociscen" before that, I said: Has he gone, has it gone? Because the purpose of my conversation with Mandic was to ask him whether he had done anything about the departure of that family mentioned before, Savic, Milos, and so on. He was talking to me about one thing, and I was talking to him about another thing, and that was to save the people who had been imprisoned on the Muslim side. I said "gone," he said "ociscen." I cannot connect what he's talking about to what I'm talking about. I know the reason I called him. There's something here in code, and I'm thinking about what it is he's saying. I'm intervening for the family of Milos Savic - he was the secretary of the Assembly - here. I'm speaking to him all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions on the intercept, as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we go, please, to the last intercept in this bundle. This is P389, KID31492. It's a conversation between you and your brother on the 10th of July of 1992. As far as the Defence are aware, this has never been played to the Court or, indeed, commented upon. Mr. Krajisnik, on the first page in the English we see that you ask your brother -- and I'm clarifying -- and I'm summarising here - about the fact you've heard some corpses were -- had been found, Serb corpses. You asked him: Where are they? And he said: Well, the Miljacka brought that down the Bosna estuary, some of it even into the Bosna and so ... You asked: Have they found ... And he said: Well, yeah, they found it. They allegedly went there on a shooting. I didn't see that, but I heard. What's that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a reference to a small river called the Miljacka which flowed to Sarajevo and flowed into the river Bosna in the Rajlovac area. As it says here, several corpses floated down this little river up to Rajlovac, which means that they had been thrown into the water. They were dead. They had been killed, and the corpses came from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Over the page we see a reference to someone called Torana. Who was Torana?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Torana -- Zoran you mean. Can you just tell me where this is -- oh, no, Tarana, Tarana. This is a typo, Torana. This was someone who had a video camera. He was supposed to film something, and he was killed during the war. I think he was working in SRNA for the television -- or I don't know exactly where.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is some reference a few lines further on to Radovanovic, and your brother is then giving you some information about Radovanovic. Who was Radovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav Radovanovic was supposed to be the commissioner for Rajlovac, Ilidza, and I don't know what other place. He was appointed as such. This is about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And your brother seems to be telling you various things about him. Why is your brother having to tell you things surrounding and to do with a commissioner?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's a telephone conversation where my brother tells me we have received the decision, but Radovanovic has not arrived. Can you get him to come? And I said I'll try. And this Miro was there, and he wanted to put me in contact with him because he was having some kind of problem. And I said: Leave that alone now. Let's talk about other things. And I spoke to Miro very briefly, as can be seen here, because -- about a certain issue because my brother wanted to inform me about the following. A delegation from Rajlovac wanted to come to Pale, and my brother says now: Miro thinks they shouldn't come. And here let him in consult you. And I said: Miro, you settle this, you're the commissioner, and that was the end of the conversation. I wasn't talking to him as a commissioner, I was talking to him because of the contact with my brother. And he was there, and he wanted to hear my opinion as to whether this delegation should go to Pale or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: If we go to the last page we see that you said, towards the end: "Such an agreement would be good, even if it became public, you know. That there's talk of the negotiations beginning and so ... That would be good. That would be useful. Mirko: Because the reason why I'm telling you is that there is a good reason to light up the people here, petitions are being collected, and so. Momcilo: Yeah. Mirko: Yeah. Momcilo: All right. That's fine. You go on and make the contact and talk. That is not a problem I need to speak to." What negotiations was there talk of beginning?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR, because there's an airport at Rajlovac, wanted to have their helicopters there. The population thought they were going to occupy the garrison and drive them out, so a petition was being signed against this. The late Mr. Nikola Koljevic was talking with General McKenzie. And there's another conversation about this, it's about the dissatisfaction of the people. A tense situation had arisen. My brother says it would be a good idea to have an agreement with the Muslim side, and their representative was this Semso, because on our side there are various people who are inflamed, meaning they could do something reckless. And what was very important for us was to have peace. Different people were spreading this information, saying: We are at war with the Muslims and we shouldn't have any kind of local agreement with them, we should simply wage war. These were not numerous, these people, they weren't the decision-makers, but they were there. And now this Semso turned up, and you saw when Mr. Sinisa Krsman was testifying here that there was always a line between the Muslims and the Serbs and that was this Semso. At one point it had been cut off because of the military activity. And now Semso was asking whether they wanted an agreement on the cessation of hostilities. And although I was not authorised to do so, I told them: Do this and publish it, so that everybody will see it's possible to have a local agreement rather than fighting. I don't know what they did later on, but peace was maintained for a long time. And I can say that the local people at Sokolje would not have fought the Muslims, but then another shift would arrive from elsewhere. And the local people would even tell the people from Zabrdje: Watch out because next week it will not be us standing guard but some people from elsewhere. And that's how more than two-thirds of Zabrdje was taken by the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm going to move away from the intercepts, and what I would now like to do is ask you about a number of Prosecution witnesses. By reason of time restriction, I'm not going to be in the position, for the most part, to put to you what these various witnesses have said about you and, in particular, against you during the course of their evidence. What I'd like you to do, Mr. Krajisnik, is give the Chamber a thumbnail sketch of your assessment back in 1991/1992 of these various people, and I'd like to begin, first of all, with Mr. Djokanovic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm glad you asked about Djokanovic first. I know everything Djokanovic said here before this Tribunal, and I can answer every question -- or rather, with respect to every question I can tell you why it's not correct. And I can point you to a document which will confirm this. Mr. Djokanovic first said that on the 10th of June he arrived in Pale, and then that he stayed at Pale for a day or two. And he knows who the members of the Presidency are and he says I was one of them. He couldn't have known this because he wasn't there before the 10th of June. And then he went out into the field and visited six municipalities where he set up commissions and he returned. And around the 15th or 16th of June he came back. He had been to Sekovici, Vlasenica, Zvornik, Bratunac, and Skelani. And there are decisions showing that he was the president and the others were members. In Zvornik he ousted the president of the municipality, and then Mr. Karadzic restored him. When he arrived on the 15th or 16th of June - he doesn't know precisely when - he says that he told the leadership that terrible things had happened in Zvornik, and he said he had told me this, too. On the 15th of June, in the minutes of the government where there was discussion of the situation in SAO Birac and a delegation was sent to investigate -- you can find those minutes. On the 30th of June, Mr. Djokanovic met Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mladic in Zvornik. And, had anything happened, he could have discussed it with them, but he says nothing was discussed. In Han Pijesak and later on in Zvornik, there was the supreme military court. He could have reported any incidents to that court. He mentions the Assembly where there was a session a year later, and I can point you to the precise place, where as a member of the government he came into conflict with a deputy from Zvornik. This deputy said that he had accused him of genocide. He said, very decidedly, that it was not true that there had been a genocide and that it wasn't true that the Serbian people are genocidal. You can see that in the Assembly where he is a deputy. If he had wanted to establish something or correct something, as a member of the government towards the end of 1992 he had the opportunity to investigate everything through the Ministry of Justice and the MUP. He could have investigated everything and established the truth. I guarantee that he never told me a single thing, nor do I know anything about this visit of his. He said that on the 10th of June or as of the 10th of June he was under my jurisdiction, I was in charge of him. From the 25th to the 27th of June you have a document where the late Mr. Koljevic signed a decision for Mrs. Plavsic appointing her. He was in charge of commissioners at the time. What is true is the following: A man from a family I know arrived from new Sarajevo. His name was Radan. I knew him, and he came together with him. And he was saying that there were problems in new Sarajevo. As I knew the man and Djokanovic was there, Djokanovic said to me: Would it be a good idea, as I hail from Novo Sarajevo, from Grbavica, for me to go there and find out what it's about? And I said it would be an excellent idea for the two you to go and see what's going on. After that, you have a decision signed by Mr. Karadzic where it says "commissioner." It doesn't say "Djokanovic," but "at the proposal of Mr. Djokanovic," and there were members of the commission. Allegedly he was the president of the commission. You remember Mr. Radomir Neskovic who says he doesn't remember when he arrived in Novo Sarajevo. That was my role. Those were my only dealings with Mr. Djokanovic. And I had another meeting with him. He came with somebody from abroad. I have noted it down somewhere. I was sitting there, and there was a man who was an acquaintance of his, and he had brought him to see me. I had no other contacts with him. Before the war he closely collaborated with Mr. Karadzic, as president of the party, and you have a number of telephone conversations, but he never contacted me. During the war he contacted Mr. Koljevic. Mr. Koljevic gathered young intellectuals around him in order to carry on academic discussions with him, and I think they discussed those topics more than they discussed commissioners. Mr. Djokanovic, as early as October, became an advisor to the late Mr. Koljevic. And there are some minutes of the so-called Presidency signed by Momcilo Krajisnik as the chairperson on the 9th of October, where you can see my signature and the Presidency is supposed to have been there. On the same date, Mr. Koljevic signed a decision that at a session of the Presidency Mr. Djokanovic had been appointed his advisor. So that session where I signed as the chairperson was not actually a session of the Presidency because that topic was not discussed at all. My conclusion is the following: This is an immature person, I have to say that, overambitious. He is a person who was scared that he would be held responsible for something. So for reasons that are unclear, he started trying to find a way out, because he was in charge of all those municipalities where terrible things happened. And I can show you all the evidence to substantiate this, Your Honours, because I have gone into a deep analysis of all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd next like to ask you about Milan Babic, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The late Milan Babic. He is deceased so I will try to choose my words about him carefully. I don't know whether I met the late Milan Babic two or three times. I never sat down with him. He said something which is completely untrue, and that's that in late 1992 I was in Novi Grad, that's Bosanski Novi, at some kind of Assembly meeting when Mr. Seselj was there. Why is this important? I was not in Bosanski Novi. Mr. Pasic said that, too, and everybody knows when this Assembly was held. It was only a year later that this Assembly was held. Seselj was there at the time, but not at the Assembly, and it's true that there was a joint Assembly of the Srpska Krajina and the Republika Srpska. But why is this point in time in 1992 so crucial? It's as if he wanted to say when ethnic cleansing was carried out, as he says, Momcilo Krajisnik was in Bosanski Novi. Mr. Seselj arrived, and together they supported ethnic cleansing. That's how I understood his malicious intentions. I wasn't there in 1992, I didn't know about the Muslims going there, I wasn't there with Mr. Seselj, and I met Mr. Babic only a few times. Why was Mr. Babic so bitter about me, if you could see that? Because the Serb delegation, including me, the people from Banja Luka, Pale, and so on, were in favour of implementing the Vance Plan, that was in early 1992, and he was profoundly opposed to it. We agreed with it. Later, he was dismissed, and he was constantly trying to separate off the Bosnian Krajina and to join up -- join it up with the Serb Krajina, which would have gone contrary to the Vance Plan. We would have been in trouble with our people who wanted to join the Serb Krajina but didn't understand politics, they didn't realise that they would be contravening two agreements and that this would be very counter-productive for them. I cannot give you any further details about him or say anything else. I can only guess what he said. He said another thing that is very important here. He said that I tried to persuade him to have the Ekavsi, E-k-a, Ekavsi, or the Cyrillic alphabet introduced. He said the Serbian people speak Ekavsi, E-k-a, Ekavsi in Serbia, and Ijekavski, I-j-e, in other parts. And when Yugoslavia collapsed, in Bosnia-Herzegovina the language was called Serbo-Croatian, so it was both Serb and Croatian. The Croats said: We have our own language, and we're not going to call it that anymore. The Muslims who didn't have a language of their own but spoke Serbo-Croatian, they called that language with some modifications the Bosniak language. So all that was left for us to do was to call our language the Serbian language, and this was at the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina when demands were made that three languages should be used, and we laughed about it because it's the same language within different nuances. So we called it the Serb language, and we said that the Ekavian and Ijekavian dialects would be equal and that the Cyrillic alphabet and the Latin alphabet would be used pursuant to the law. And he made use of this to say that I was in favour of some kind of separatism, and this was very improper, because everybody else did the same before the Serbs called their language the Serbian language. I don't know whether he said anything else. We met only two or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next witness I want to ask you about is Boro Bjelobrk. Much of his evidence dealt with his assessment of the SDS in the years, or months perhaps I should say, leading up to the war. Of course, you have dealt with that in some detail during the course of the questions that Mr. Stewart has asked you. But notwithstanding that, what comments do you have about Mr. Bjelobrk?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Although I don't like to speak badly of people, with full responsibility I can say that Mr. Bjelobrk is a communist. He lived in the communist system, and he was privileged in it. Ideologically he was bitterly opposed to any national parties. Why was he not equally opposed to the Muslim national party with the same vehemence? Because in the former system there was a quota system, and if a Muslim was at the head, then his deputy would have to be a Serb or a Croat. So the ethnic make-up was always taken into account, in every commercial enterprise, in every institution, everywhere. The posts that belonged to the Serbs, even though, as he says himself, was a Yugoslav -- he calls himself a Yugoslav, although he's from a Serb family, he always held the post reserved for a Serb everywhere. Now that the national parties had emerged, it suited him to have the Serbs in a minority somewhere, because as part of a minority he would be able to take up the Serb post. When the Serb parties arrived, of course other people would be holding those posts. One thing he said here which is very important is that ideologically he hated the Serb Democratic Party and the national parties. Unfortunately, I don't want to go into private matters and tell you who he's married to, but he had this resistance. Your Honours, I have shown you what his error was. Once I was left on my own in parliament. The Serbs deputies had left, and I voted in favour of an item on the agenda, and later on the vote was against and they needed one more vote for their item to be put on the agenda. And I voted in favour, so their item was included in the agenda, thanks to my vote. I was the only Serb from the SDS. When the discussion was over, we counted the votes. There were 130, and there was one vote missing, and I said: I give them my vote, the 131st. When their item on the agenda came up for voting, we counted the votes and there were 134, so my vote was not necessary for their item to be adopted. It was a benign item. And even though it was imposed by force, I said: I will now abstain. There's no need for me to vote in favour. Well, now he describes this as my duplicity. And before that all the SDS deputies had left that Assembly meeting. They were very upset because something that had been agreed beforehand had not been respected. Everything he says about these territories are his own hallucinations. He is a man suffering from ideological blindness. He remained in the central part of Sarajevo, and he's constantly jockeying for position because there are few Serbs there, so he wants to be appointed to various posts. Before he used to be in the trade union. He just wants to have a post and privileges and, unfortunately, he does have that in the Muslim part of Sarajevo. I have had very little contact with him. They had another president of the deputies club, also a Serb, Miro Lazovic, who is no better than him; on the contrary, they're the same. But it was Miro Lazovic I had contacts with. I rarely contacted with Bjelobrk in those groups, so to say. If Your Honours remember, he gave an example. I was the president of the Assembly, and he brought a trade union delegation for me to intervene in Yugoslavia, in Belgrade, to have an invoice of theirs paid. This has nothing to do with president of the Assembly, and they say that I was hostile. But he was bringing these dissatisfied trade unionists in order to turn them against me, saying: You see, here is this Serb who is representing this group and nothing he said is correct. I have even prepared a CD for Their Honours with the dates of the discussions, and showing how the discussions were led. He complained because I had had prolonged sessions, but I was trying not to have the Assembly divided. There were pauses and so on, but that was my goal, not to obstruct the work of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Just clarify this. The CD you have just referred to, what's that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Honourable Presiding Judge and the Honourable Judge Canivell remember when I handed over three CDs to you and then you returned them to me when Mr. Bjelobrk was being discussed and you didn't really look at it. And I did that before the Honourable Judge Hanoteau came. So that was returned and all of that is mentioned on those CDs, but this is a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next person I'd like to talk -- turn to, please, is Mr. Kljujic. I have asked you a number of questions about him, and put to you during the course of your review of some of the intercepts in which you were a participant, assertions by Mr. Kljujic, and you have dealt with those. In fact, earlier today you dealt with his assertion, for example, that you were fully informed about ethnic cleansing that was occurring in Bosnia in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kljujic was interpreting that telephone conversation, and he says this shows that Mr. Krajisnik knew about ethnic cleansing. I would like to remind you of the following now. Mr. Kljujic said here that he was the president of the state commission for establishing war crimes, that is to say, war crimes committed by all sides. So he didn't establish any of these and he wasn't involved in that. Truth to tell, he was a member of the Presidency until the end of 1991 and then the Presidency replaced him with Miro Lasic. And then he was returned yet again because of Miro Lasic, because Miro Lasic had left the Presidency, that is. Mr. Kljujic was president of the HDZ, the Croatian Democratic Union. All communications before the war, up to the war, that is to say during the election campaign as well, he carried out at the level of party president. He confirmed that himself. As for my own contacts with Mr. Kljujic --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Can I stop you. Before we get on to that, clarification please. You said, I quote: "Mr. Kljujic said here that he was president of the state commission for establishing war crimes, that is to say, war crimes committed by all sides. So he didn't establish any of these and he wasn't involved in that." That's the end of the quote. What did you mean by: "So he didn't establish any of these and he wasn't involved in that"?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not the way I put it, but it was similar, though. Mr. Kljujic stated here that he was president of the commission for establishing war crimes -- the state commission, that is, the state commission of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was in Sarajevo. During that time, since he headed this state commission, he was supposed to establish what kind of crimes were committed against all ethnic groups. I'm just giving an example. Today we have a list of missing persons, and I know that he did not establish any crimes that had been committed against the Serbs, not even against the Croats. He only worked on seeing what crimes were committed against Muslims, if he did anything at all. And I said that he was there only until the end of 1992. For a while he was replaced by Miro Lasic, and I don't know what he did after that. He was not a member of that commission. And I said that I did not have much contact with him and I did not really contact him or talk to him. And it's not true that that meeting was held in my office the way he represents it, where Stanic was and others. In my office, there was this one chair, and there were two chairs on the sides. It wasn't that three plus three people could sit there, so there was sort of the president and a table and these two chairs. So you could not really have three Serbs and three Croats sitting there. Anybody can establish that; that's probably the way it is to this day. So it could not have happened there, and I do not know what he's talking about. Physically it was not possible. Maybe somebody else had a meeting during one of the breaks. I don't know about that, I'm not aware of that, I don't remember that, but it certainly wasn't in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd next like to move on to Miroslav Deronjic. Part of his evidence dealt with events within the SDS in October, November, and December of 1991. Can I -- I'm not going to ask you about that and don't really want you to comment on his assertions in that regard because you have dealt with that in another part of your evidence. What contact did you have with Mr. Deronjic in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember contacts with him. I mean, I knew of him, and I had a very good opinion of Mr. Deronjic at the time, but I cannot remember whether I had any contact with him at the time. I did not have any contact with him as a member of the appointments commission because it did not meet and work. I did not have contacts at the Main Board because sessions were not being held. Possibly when there was some joint meeting of all that he was present there, but I did not talk to him specifically -- or perhaps I talked to him a minute somewhere, but I cannot remember. His activities were primarily party-based, and he talked to people who had duties within the party. I can give comments regarding his statement, if you're interested.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I want to ask you specifically about something he did say in the course of his evidence on the 19th of February of 2004 at page 1223, and that related to the opening of a corridor between Bratunac and Kravica. And he said that that would have to have been approved by the top leadership of the Republika Srpska. And he said it was a Mr. Zekic who gave approval. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I do not remember this particular wording, but I remember that he referred to Zekic as his mentor and his main connection between him and the leadership of Republika Srpska. That was to say that he got some sort of message from the late Mr. Zekic that this action could be carried through. I cannot confirm that. I cannot deny that, but I can indicate something illogical that he said and that brings into question the authenticity of his decision. He said that he was the connection for A and B variants, Variants A and B, and that a Serb municipality of Srebrenica was not established by Zekic because he was not organised. But I would like to remind you of the document you have. Mr. Grkovic's diary of the 20th of December, where it is written, recorded, a decision came in on the establishment of the Serb Assembly of Srebrenica. That is to say, that he did not even know that Zekic had, before that, before these Variants A and B were there, that he had actually established already this Serb municipality of Srebrenica. I'm trying to say -- well, I have to make the following comment. He said many things here in order to make his own situation easier, especially referring to people who died or who he believes will never come before this Hague Tribunal. Remember that he said that 50 kilometres from the Drina left and right were supposed to be Serb territory. If it were to be 50 kilometres, then the border would have to be by Tuzla. Only an insane person could say that. It isn't even 50 kilometres from the Drina to Tuzla. So half of Bosnia would have to be taken in order to have this Serb belt. You also saw the public denial of Rajko Dukic after his statement here that he never talked to him about this, but I really cannot comment on any other details. I mean, I'd have to engage in guesswork.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When did you become aware of the massacre in Glogova that Mr. Deronjic being part of?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the war, I never knew of this crime in Glogova. I met him and he never told me that there had been a massacre there. Quite simply, as he had put it, Glogova had been liberated; everybody was saying that. I had never heard of this story of his before. I don't know whether he met anyone at that meeting, but I assure you that if any crime had been committed, people concealed that and they didn't want to brag about it. On the contrary. An investigation would have to be carried out in order to establish whether somebody had done something or not. When I saw what this was all about here, I was surprised as everyone else who was present. I just have to tell you one more thing. There is a record here of the court questioning him as an accused person. During the war, I got this later, Zekic's father accuses him of having betrayed Zekic, and in that record he talks about Glogova, about what happened. I got that only the other day. That is to say, that somebody knew about that. He talked about all of this that happened in Glogova during the war, but I -- or someone else from our ranks -- well, I didn't know about it. In that statement that he made during the course of the war, he probably stated that to some municipal court or I don't know who. I have this document here, I can present it. It was only the other day that I got this document. I never had it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm in the Chamber's hands, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it depends what -- Mr. Krajisnik, could you briefly describe what that document is you're referring to. Is it a statement? Is it -- first of all, from what date is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a record, Your Honour, of a court hearing of the different parties involved. Perhaps I even have it here with me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I asked you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- what's the date. Clear question. Please stop explaining what the document is. If you know, please tell us; if you don't know, I'll put my next question to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know, I'd have to look it up. But I think it was during the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please look it up, and if you have the dates tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll look it up straight away, and if I haven't got it here, I'll bring it in tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I was going to suggest that Mr. Krajisnik does this overnight and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I can imagine. Mr. Krajisnik, you're invited to do that overnight, and then it will not take court time. So if you find it this evening, you could tell us tomorrow in three lines what exactly it is. Please proceed, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to go into private --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've got me so scared that I don't know -- well, all right. I'll find it tonight and I'll bring it tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'd like to go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Krajisnik, there's one small issue, I wouldn't say a very important one, but which we'd like to address in your absence, you being the witness at this moment. So therefore, I'd like to invite you to be escorted out of the courtroom so that I can address the matter. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just ask you something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said about this CD --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you were about to ask me something, that's at least how it was. You said: "Could I just ask you something?" And then I said: "Yes." And then it was interpreted -- Could you please put your earphones on again? Mr. Krajisnik, at this moment in the transcript I read that you said to me: "Could I just ask you something?" I said: "Yes." And then your words were translated as: "You said about this CD --" and there it stops. So if you want to ask us something, I wished to give you an opportunity to do so, but I didn't hear any question there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I looked at this CD -- or rather, this DVD yesterday. It has to do with that interview of mine, but there is another segment there that's -- that is important, and you said that they should look at it in the meantime and that it should be admitted into evidence here. It has to do with the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I invited the parties to look at it and to answer the question, so I take it that we -- we'll hear from either Mr. -- either the Prosecution and Defence or both by tomorrow. Would that be a --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just say something? It's minute 49, seconds 15. It's going to make it easier for them to find it. The 49th minute, 15th second states exactly what the members of the Presidency are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take that that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we have no [indiscernible], Your Honours. Your Honour, can I just say that this -- we're not intending to be unnecessarily difficult. We don't know what the issue is. It's taken us slightly by surprise that Mr. Krajisnik's being asked to leave. Your Honour, we would just like to reserve our position formally in relation to that, because it's something we don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's not a big issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But nevertheless to be dealt with in the absence of Mr. Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know what you're going to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the issue is -- it's -- I don't think it's a very -- Mr. Josse, we have some of these informal translations of documents which were introduced very quickly. We just wanted to let you know that it's not entirely clear to the Chamber what purpose they serve exactly. For example, if I just take one example, D223, which bears the signature of Mr. Davidovic says something about a car which was inspected, apart from -- even if we would follow what Mr. Krajisnik said, that it must have been seized, although the document doesn't say that. We have some difficulties in understanding exactly what the purpose of this is when I do remember well Mr. Davidovic said something about vehicles which were seized and then sold by I think members of the MUP or the SUP; I don't know exactly what it was. Here this document tells us that the vehicles should be registered for purposes of the Serbian MUP. I think Mr. Davidovic never said anything of the kind, that those vehicles should not be used for official purposes or whatever. He said something about personal profit taken by -- by members of the MUP -- I think it's not all clear in my recollection, but something that they sold them to their own profit. So, therefore, such a report is hanging, more or less, in the air. To some extent, it would confirm what Mr. Davidovic said. If you would interpret such a document as saying: Here you see that if they were later on sold, that Mr. Davidovic himself contributed to that course, but that's of course an interpretation. We have not fully understood the -- the true meaning of these documents and how we should interpret them. We just wanted you to -- to let you know so that if you have to spend time on further examination, or, Mr. Stewart, that you would at least be aware that it did not fully come to an understanding within the Chamber. And we leave it up to you whether it's important enough to pay further attention to or whether you would say: Well, it's perhaps not of that vital importance for the case, that even if we would not understand every single bit of this part of the evidence, that it would not damage your case. We leave that to you, but we did not want to say this in the presence of Mr. Krajisnik because it might have caused him to explain a lot of things on which you, as counsel, might think that there are other matters more important perhaps to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, speaking about it for myself without speaking to Mr. Stewart --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: -- first of all, let me say I take Your Honour's comments in the spirit in which they were clearly intended, i.e., to be helpful, and I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm bound to say it comes as great concern to me that this has been done in Mr. Krajisnik's absence. I don't really follow why, but perhaps we can think about this overnight --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The main purpose being --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because I'm not sure there is any provision for it all. In a common law system, Your Honour, it would be quite impossible, let me say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you know that we are not in a common law system.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, if finally there's nothing -- I think, as a matter of fact, we just discussed whether it should be on the DVD that Mr. Krajisnik receives tomorrow, but he will receive it, but at the end of his testimony. What we wanted to avoid is that we get here a clash of what is most important to use Defence time for.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I certainly take the position that we'd rather not have such a battle here and rather use the time as efficiently as possible. And we still, as you may have noticed in the past, we still think that counsel has an important, if not very important, if not a decisive role in prioritising these matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure both of us take this, as I've already said, in the spirit in which it is intended, and we're grateful to the Chamber for these words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you find it important enough to make us further explore the common law tradition in this respect, we are willing to do so. We're not encouraging you to do so, not because we think it's improper to do, but in view of the matter at stake and in view of how we usually deal with matters in the presence of Mr. Krajisnik. I would be surprised, but I can -- it could be a mistake on my side that it has not a great bearing on what happens at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: With respect, I agree, but we will reserve our position. I would like to talk to Mr. Stewart about what has just happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. If there's any need, we'll hear from you further. I apologise to the technicians and the interpreters, where I thought that I had improved my record in late finishes, I'm afraid that this is a major fall back on that. We'll adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past 2.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
